title: How Bitcoin Actually Works (Explained Simply)

beats.text: In twenty ten, a man paid ten thousand bitcoin for two pizzas. Today, those coins would be worth about eight hundred and forty million dollars.
Now look at Dave's cousin, Kevin. Last October, Kevin bought bitcoin at the very top. One hundred and twenty six thousand dollars per coin.
Today, one bitcoin is worth about eighty four thousand. Kevin has lost about a third of his money. And he calls Dave every single night.
So Dave has questions. What even is bitcoin? Who controls it? And why does the price go completely crazy?
And it gets stranger. Nobody knows who invented it.
Today: the shared notebook, the puzzle lottery, the twenty one million limit, and how not to end up like Kevin.
Let's start with a mystery.
On October thirty first, two thousand eight, someone calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto posted a short paper online. Just nine pages.
The title: Bitcoin, a peer to peer electronic cash system. In plain words: money you can send to anyone, with no bank in the middle.
Why would anyone want that? Well, right then, the world was in a huge financial crisis. Banks were collapsing, and trust in them was at rock bottom.
In January two thousand nine, the bitcoin network switched on. A couple of years later, Satoshi simply disappeared. Nobody knows who it was, even today.
Imagine inventing a whole new kind of money, and then just walking away.
So how can money work with no bank? Let's use a notebook.
Normally, the bank keeps one notebook. It says: Dave has one hundred dollars. Grandma has fifty. And only the bank can write in it.
Bitcoin's idea: give a copy of the notebook to everyone. Thousands of computers all over the world, each with the exact same copy.
When Dave sends one coin to Grandma, he shouts it to everyone. Dave pays Grandma one bitcoin. And every copy of the notebook adds the new line.
Can Dave cheat, and write: I have a million coins? No. Everyone else checks their copy and says: nope, that's not what our notebook says.
That shared notebook has a fancy name. The blockchain. The pages are called blocks, and they're chained together, in order.
And Dave doesn't sign with a pen. He signs with a secret code called a private key. Remember that. It matters later.
But wait. If everyone has a notebook, who gets to write the next page?
That's what mining is. And no, there are no shovels.
About every ten minutes, special computers race to solve a puzzle. It's really a guessing game. Guess a number. Wrong. Guess again. Trillions of times per second.
Think of a giant lottery. Every guess is a ticket. The more computers you own, the more tickets you get.
The winner writes the next page of the notebook. And as a prize, they get brand new bitcoin. That's how new coins are born.
Why the puzzle? Because it makes cheating super expensive. To rewrite the notebook, you'd have to win the lottery again and again, against the whole world.
Now here's the part fans love. There will only ever be twenty one million bitcoin. Ever.
Remember the duck from our very first video? Banks can create new money out of nothing. Bitcoin can't. The limit is written into the code.
And the miners' prize keeps shrinking. About every four years, it gets cut in half. This is called the halving.
In two thousand nine, the prize was fifty bitcoin per page. Then twenty five. Then twelve and a half. Then six point two five.
The latest halving was in April twenty twenty four. Now the prize is just three point one two five bitcoin.
In March this year, the twenty millionth bitcoin was mined. The last million will trickle out slower and slower, until around the year twenty one forty.
It's a bit like gold, from our gold video. Hard to get, and the supply grows slower every year.
So what is one bitcoin actually worth? At first, almost nothing.
On May twenty second, twenty ten, a programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz wanted pizza. He offered ten thousand bitcoin to anyone who'd bring him two. Someone did.
Those two pizzas cost about forty dollars. It was the first famous time bitcoin bought something real. Fans still celebrate it every year. Bitcoin Pizza Day.
Then the price started climbing. About one thousand dollars in twenty thirteen. Nearly twenty thousand in twenty seventeen. Sixty nine thousand in twenty twenty one.
And in October twenty twenty five, a new record. About one hundred and twenty six thousand dollars for a single coin.
As we make this video, in late September twenty twenty six, one bitcoin is around eighty four thousand dollars.
Which makes those two pizzas worth about eight hundred and forty million dollars. The most expensive dinner in history.
But the price doesn't go up in a straight line. It goes up like a roller coaster. And down like one too.
In twenty twenty one, bitcoin hit sixty nine thousand. One year later, it was around sixteen thousand. A drop of more than seventy five percent.
Why so wild? Because nothing sets the price except people buying and selling. No company profits. No interest. Just what the next person will pay.
Then, in January twenty twenty four, something big happened. The American regulator, the S E C, approved eleven bitcoin E T Fs.
An E T F lets you buy bitcoin through a normal investment account, just like buying a share. Big investors poured in, and the price climbed.
But the regulator was careful to say: we approved the funds, not bitcoin itself. It's still very risky.
And that brings us back to Kevin. Last October, everyone was talking about bitcoin. His friends. The news. Kevin felt he was missing out.
So he put in ten thousand dollars, right at the top. Today, it's worth about six thousand seven hundred. Kevin bought the hype, not the coin.
Now, the dark side. Remember the secret code, the private key?
If you lose it, your bitcoin is gone. Forever. No bank to call. No forgot password button.
Researchers at Chainalysis estimate that between two point three and three point seven million bitcoin are probably lost for good. That's up to one in every six coins.
One man in Wales says he threw away an old hard drive with eight thousand bitcoin on it. It's somewhere in a landfill. He spent years trying to dig it up.
And then there are scammers. In twenty twenty five, Americans reported losing eleven point four billion dollars to crypto fraud, according to the F B I. A record.
Fake investment apps. Online romances that turn into: let me help you invest. And fake helpers who promise to get your lost money back.
Remember the raccoon? He found a brand new costume.
One more big debate. That puzzle lottery uses a lot of electricity.
A Cambridge University report estimated that bitcoin mining uses about one hundred and thirty eight terawatt hours a year. That's around half a percent of all the world's electricity.
Critics say: that's a lot of power for a guessing game. It adds pollution, and it can strain local power grids.
Supporters answer: more than half of mining now uses sustainable energy, like hydro, wind and nuclear. And miners often use cheap power that would otherwise go to waste.
Is it worth it? That depends on whether you think bitcoin is useful. Smart people disagree. But now you know the numbers.
So what does Dave tell Kevin? Education, not advice.
One. Never invest money you can't afford to lose. Bitcoin has dropped by more than half several times. It can happen again.
Two. When you hear that everyone is getting rich, be careful. That's often close to the top. Just ask Kevin.
Three. Beware of scams. Nobody honest will ever ask for your private key. And guaranteed returns in crypto don't exist.
Four. Understand what you buy. If you can't explain it to a friend, like we just did with the notebook, slow down.
And Kevin? He decided to stop checking the price every hour. His blood pressure says thank you.
So let's recap.
One. Bitcoin is a shared notebook that thousands of computers keep together, with no bank in the middle.
Two. Miners win a puzzle lottery to write each page. The prize halves about every four years, and there will never be more than twenty one million coins.
Three. The price is wild, scams are everywhere, and a lost key means lost money.
